sources.title: Slice vs Drop Shot Technique | DROP SHOTS
TENNIS DROP SHOT | How To Hit A Drop Shot - Tennis Evolution

good_form: Play the drop shot from around the baseline or once you're inside the court, when the ball you get is shorter.
Pick the longer-trajectory drop shot, played off a normal-height slice, when you want a safer option. The opponent sees the change in flight later.
Use that safer, pushed-short version when the opponent is stretched wide and can't reach it. Don't try a high, very short ball.
Stay calm and precise. Play drop shots when the score is in your favour and you feel no pressure.
Play it off a ball with topspin, or a normal flat ball that spins forward after the bounce, but not heavy topspin. Avoid slice balls where you can.
Play it off a ball that arrives with some pace.
The wrong-footing drop shot is the most effective. Hit it back to where the opponent just came from, because changing direction is very hard.
Play a drop shot off a high ball only when you're very close to the net or service line, on a very short ball.

faults.name: Drop shot from far behind the baseline
faults.looks_like: Hitting the drop shot from behind or well behind the baseline.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball stays in the air longer, so the opponent has more time to reach it.
causes: Playing it from too deep a position.
fixes: From behind the baseline, play a slice and keep the ball deep.
Wait for a shorter ball and play the drop shot once you can get into the court.
outcome_effects: The ball flies a long way and the opponent gets to it easily.

faults.name: Trying a very short, high-trajectory drop shot
faults.looks_like: Lofting the ball high so it lands very short.
faults.why_it_matters: It is the riskiest option. The trajectory is hard to find and experienced players read it quickly.
causes: Aiming for the shortest possible drop shot.
A higher ball flight that gives the shot away.
fixes: Play the longer, lower version off a slice that looks like a normal ball.
Don't use the very short version unless the situation is perfect.
outcome_effects: The opponent starts running early and reaches the ball.
If the ball lands any deeper, you lose the point.

faults.name: Playing the drop shot when nervous or under pressure
faults.looks_like: Hitting a drop shot while feeling stressed, anxious or tight, for example at 30-all.
faults.why_it_matters: The shot is double-edged and needs precision. Nerves make that precision unlikely.
causes: Stress or anxiety.
A close or unfavourable score.
fixes: Check how you feel first.
Play drop shots when ahead, such as at 40-love, 40-15 or early in the game.
outcome_effects: Too short and you hit the net.
Too high and long and the opponent gets an easy short ball. Either way you likely lose the point.

faults.name: Drop shot off an incoming slice
faults.looks_like: Trying a drop shot on a slice ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It is harder to do accurately.
causes: It is hard to judge how much force a slice needs.
fixes: Choose a flat or topspin ball instead.
Wait for the right situation.
Use it only if the opponent is well out of position and you don't need much precision.
outcome_effects: You are likely to mis-hit the ball.

faults.name: Drop shot off a high ball
faults.looks_like: Hitting a drop shot at a higher contact point.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball tends to bounce high and fly longer, giving the opponent time.
causes: Contact point is high.
Standing further back.
fixes: Do it only when very close to the net or service line, on a very short ball.
outcome_effects: The ball flies long and the opponent reaches it with an easy jog.

faults.name: Drop shot off a dead ball
faults.looks_like: Trying a drop shot when the incoming ball has almost no pace.
faults.why_it_matters: It is much harder than with a ball that has some speed.
causes: The incoming ball has very little speed.
fixes: Prefer a ball that arrives with some pace.

good_form: When the opponent drops or the ball dribbles over the net, answer a drop shot with your own drop shot.
Start running forward right away and pump your arms.
Keep the racket out in front of you while you run, not behind you.
Advanced players can run in with a topspin (semi-western) grip, strings pointing down, so the opponent expects a hard topspin shot.
At the last moment, switch to a volley grip using only the hitting hand, with the non-hitting hand off the racket, to disguise the drop shot.
Open the racket face and barely move the racket.
Keep the feet moving so the racket's momentum comes from the feet rather than the arm, which lets you hit softly.
Put a little backspin on the ball so it dies after landing and bounces twice before the opponent can reach it.

faults.name: Racket pulled back while running forward
faults.looks_like: Running toward a drop shot with the racket held behind the body, like a relay runner holding a baton.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you running your fastest and leaves you only able to hit the ball hard when you arrive.
causes: Taking the racket back early as you run toward the short ball
fixes: Keep the racket in front of you as you run
Pump your arms while running
Run with the topspin grip and change grip late if you want to disguise the shot
outcome_effects: You can't get to the ball as quickly
You can only hit the ball hard instead of a soft drop shot

good_form: Hold the racket with a looser grip so the string bed can absorb the ball, like in the catching exercise.
Feel needs reduced speed; hitting hard makes the ball leave the strings too fast to feel.
On drop shots from farther back in the court, use more of a downward and across movement.
At the net against a pacey ball, absorb it into the strings and let the racket move backward with the ball.
A well-absorbed drop shot carries a lot of backspin, bounces on the other side and can come back toward you.
To get that bounce-back, make no forward racket movement; go slightly backward while moving down and across.
Feel is learned by practice; drills like bouncing the ball on the strings, catching a dropped ball on the strings, and mini tennis build it.
In the catch drill, the racket travels in the same direction as the ball, which slows it and stops it on the strings.

faults.name: Racket bounces the ball off on catch/absorb
faults.looks_like: When trying to catch or stop the ball on the strings, the ball bounces off the string bed instead of stopping.
faults.why_it_matters: It shows a lack of the absorbing feel needed for drop shots and other touch shots.
causes: The racket is not moving in the same direction as the ball.
The racket movement is too slow or too big against a fast ball.
fixes: Move the racket in the direction of the ball, which slows it and stops it on the strings.
For a ball with lots of pace, use a quick, small move backward rather than going far back.
outcome_effects: The ball bounces off the strings instead of stopping.

faults.name: Moving the racket forward on the drop shot
faults.looks_like: The racket goes forward into the ball on a drop shot instead of absorbing it and going slightly backward.
faults.why_it_matters: Forward racket movement stops the ball from getting the backspin and soft landing that make the ball bounce back.
causes: Not absorbing the ball into the string bed.
fixes: Absorb the ball into the strings and go slightly backward while moving down and across.
outcome_effects: The ball doesn't bounce on the other side and come back to your side.

faults.name: Gripping too tightly
faults.looks_like: A firm, tight hold on the racket grip during touch shots.
faults.why_it_matters: A tight grip prevents the string bed from absorbing the ball.
fixes: Hold the grip looser, with the mental image of absorbing the ball in the strings.

faults.name: Jerky hand movement
faults.looks_like: Beginners make jerky movements when bouncing the ball on the strings.
faults.why_it_matters: It leads to quickly losing control of the ball.
causes: Poor control of the hand.
fixes: Practice bouncing the ball on the strings and on the ground to develop a still hand and string-bed control.
outcome_effects: The ball gets away from the player.

good_form: When you reach the opponent's drop shot first, the safest reply is a deep shot down the line, then cover the net.
A counter drop shot is another option, but it needs quick thinking while you run in, because you must sense what position you will end up in.
Only try the counter drop shot when you get to the ball fairly comfortably. That is when you have the feel and precision for it.
After your counter drop shot, move forward and cover the net.
The speaker suggests the counter drop shot only for advanced players, around 4.0 to 4.5.

faults.name: Cross-court reply to a drop shot
faults.looks_like: Playing the ball cross-court when you are close to the net after reaching the drop shot.
faults.why_it_matters: You can't cover the net after a cross-court shot, unless you expect to finish the point with it.
causes: Choosing cross-court from a position close to the net
fixes: Hit deep down the line and then cover the net.
outcome_effects: You can't cover the net after the shot.

faults.name: Counter drop shot while stretched or on the run
faults.looks_like: Attempting a counter drop shot when you reach the ball at full stretch, still running, in a difficult position.
faults.why_it_matters: You lack the feel and precision the shot needs.
causes: Reaching the ball late and at full stretch
Still running and in a difficult situation when you hit
fixes: Attempt the counter drop shot only when you reach the ball fairly comfortably.
Otherwise play the safer deep shot down the line.
outcome_effects: Poor precision on the shot.

faults.name: Weak counter drop shot
faults.looks_like: Hitting a counter drop shot that isn't really good, then moving in to cover the net.
faults.why_it_matters: The counter drop shot is a double-edged sword. A poor one leaves you exposed.
causes: Not hitting a really good drop shot
fixes: Reserve the counter drop shot for advanced players and for comfortable reaches.
outcome_effects: You become a sitting duck at the net.

good_form: Move up to the ball as soon as the opponent's ball is short (the 'magnet move') instead of waiting.
Hit the drop shot while the ball is rising after the bounce, not on its way down.
Prepare exactly as for a normal forehand or backhand, with the racket head above the ball, so the opponent can't read it.
Change grip at the last moment from the normal forehand grip to a neutral grip (same from backhand); it can be done one-handed.
Racket head goes forward and under the ball rather than back, cutting it to create spin with a curved path under the ball.
Make a slow, gentle touch motion, like touching a little bird you don't want to hurt.
After contact, the back leg comes through together with the front leg and ends in front of it; hand and body move together.
Hit it from an offensive position, ideally when the opponent is moving or leaning back and on his heels, to wrong-foot him.
Stay calm and controlled so you can feel the opponent's movement and read the court.
After the shot, go to the net just in front of the service line and follow the ball's direction (down the line or cross).
A good drop shot bounces three or more times before crossing the service line; two is average, one is bad.

faults.name: Waiting for the ball (static)
faults.looks_like: Player stands still and waits for the ball instead of moving forward to it, hitting it as it drops down after the bounce.
faults.why_it_matters: Waiting gives the opponent time to recover and move back and be balanced; moving in takes time away from him.
causes: Staying static and waiting for the ball
fixes: Move up to the ball as soon as you see a short ball (magnet move).
Check that you hit the ball on the rise.
Practise with a coach feeding short balls so you take one or two steps forward and hit on the rise each time.
outcome_effects: Opponent has time to move back and get balanced, so the drop shot is less effective.

faults.name: Rushing or being excited
faults.looks_like: Acting fast and excitedly when hitting the drop shot.
faults.why_it_matters: The motion must be a calm, controlled touch motion, and you need to be aware of where the opponent is and how he is moving.
causes: Excitement and rushing
fixes: Stay as calm as possible and make the motion slow and controlled.

faults.name: Telegraphing the shot with a different preparation
faults.looks_like: Preparation that differs from a normal forehand or backhand.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent can guess a drop shot is coming.
fixes: Prepare exactly as for a normal forehand or backhand, with racket head above the ball, and change grip only at the last moment.
outcome_effects: Opponent can anticipate the drop shot.

good_form: Set up the drop shot with the previous shot: hit a high, deep ball (e.g. topspin to a one-hander's backhand) to push the opponent back.
The drop shot is much easier when the opponent is deep behind the baseline; if they stand on the baseline you'd need to be Djokovic-level.
Use volley technique: keep the racket out in front and short, with no backswing.
Aim to take pace off the ball rather than hit it hard.
Use your volley grip on both forehand and backhand drop shots.
Add only a little backspin; a low to moderate amount is enough to check the ball.
Picture the ball peaking on your side of the net and descending as it crosses the net so it lands short.
Pushing the opponent back means you don't need the ball to die like Federer's; it doesn't need perfect spin.

faults.name: Hitting the drop shot in isolation
faults.looks_like: Playing the drop shot without setting it up, often against an opponent who is standing on or near the baseline.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent can run it down easily; it takes an exceptional shot to beat someone close to the baseline.
causes: Not setting it up with the previous shot
Opponent not pushed back
fixes: Hit a high, deep ball first to push the opponent back, then use the drop shot when the reply comes from far back
Try drop shots against opponents who back up when hit a high ball
outcome_effects: Opponent reaches the ball and gets it back

faults.name: Swinging too hard / taking a backswing
faults.looks_like: Taking a backswing and hitting the ball with pace instead of using a short volley motion in front.
faults.why_it_matters: The goal is to take pace off the ball, and players often know this but don't do it.
causes: Not thinking of it like a volley
fixes: Use volley technique with the racket staying out in front
Use a very short motion with no backswing
outcome_effects: Ball carries too much pace and is not short enough

faults.name: Chopping too much backspin
faults.looks_like: Trying to chop heavily under the ball to make it stop or spin back toward the net.
faults.why_it_matters: It isn't needed and won't help consistency.
causes: Believing you need Federer-style perfect spin to make the ball die
fixes: Use only a tiny to moderate amount of backspin
Rely on pushing the opponent back so a little backspin is enough
outcome_effects: Drop shot is less consistent

faults.name: Ball not peaking on your side
faults.looks_like: The ball is still rising or travelling high as it reaches the net, so it barely clears the net or lands too deep.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball must land short enough that the opponent can't run it down.
causes: Not picturing the ball's flight path
fixes: Think of the ball peaking on your side and dropping as it crosses the net
outcome_effects: Ball lands too deep and is easier to run down
Ball barely reaches the net

good_form: The aim is for the ball to stop as soon as possible after landing, so cut the ball with backspin, a bit like a volley with extra spin.
Keep the ball on the racket as long as you can for control; don't think a longer hold sends it further.
Be fast with the legs and slow, soft and subtle with the hand, like caressing the ball or holding a small bird you don't want to hurt.
Keep moving and take at least one step after contact. Don't stop before the ball, as at the net.
Bring the ball over the net with your legs rather than your hand. The racket should feel as if it passes the ball, with the ball behind it.
Keep the ball low over the net, because height gives the opponent more time.
Point the racket head in the direction you want the ball to go: cross-court or down the line.
Don't try to hit harder. Use the same gentle, small acceleration.
Use the right grip for the shot.
Use a target and count the bounces before the ball reaches a line. More bounces, or more rolling, means a better shot.

For tactics, play it from inside the court when you could hit a winner, ideally when the opponent is moving back. Against a player on the backhand side, drop it to their forehand side to make the distance longer.

faults.name: Ball runs on instead of stopping
faults.looks_like: The ball is hit too flat and keeps going after it bounces, or it never stops short.
faults.why_it_matters: The drop shot is meant to die, and a ball that carries forward gives the opponent a chance to reach it.
causes: Not enough cut or backspin
Ball hit too flat
fixes: Cut the ball with backspin so it kicks up and stops.
Add a bit more backspin, even if it goes too high at first.
Practise with one ball and backspin, then check that it stops once it passes the net.
outcome_effects: Ball continues forward after landing
Opponent has more chance to get it

faults.name: Stopping the legs at contact
faults.looks_like: The player runs in, then stops before hitting, with no step after the shot.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact time and control suffer, and the ball can fly.
causes: Halting movement before contact
Leaving the work to the hand
fixes: Take at least one step after the shot and follow through.
Move fast with the legs and keep the hand slow.
Feel that the legs bring the ball over the net.
outcome_effects: Ball flies
Less control

faults.name: Ball too high
faults.looks_like: The ball crosses the net high.
faults.why_it_matters: The higher it is, the more time the opponent has to reach it.
causes: Trying to cut it too much, as in the forehand example
fixes: Aim to make it as low as possible over the net.
Don't judge yourself harshly: if the spin was right, just lower the next one.
outcome_effects: Opponent gets more time to run to the ball

faults.name: Using the hand too much / pushing it
faults.looks_like: The hand does too much work, with a hard hit or a thrust, and the player wants to see the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It reduces subtlety and control, and the ball goes too far.
causes: Wanting to see the ball
Trying to hit harder
fixes: Keep the hand slow and soft.
Let the legs bring the ball over.
Hold the ball on the strings longer.
outcome_effects: Ball fails to stop or goes long
Ball doesn't cross the line as planned

faults.name: Racket not going toward the target
faults.looks_like: The hand drifts and the racket head doesn't go in the intended direction.
faults.why_it_matters: It costs direction and control.
causes: Hand drifting away from the intended line
fixes: Make sure the racket head goes toward where you want to play: cross or down the line.
outcome_effects: Less accurate direction

faults.name: Playing the drop shot at the wrong time
faults.looks_like: Using it when unsure, uncomfortable or hoping for an easy point.
faults.why_it_matters: It is an aggressive shot and should be played only when you are inside the court and could hit a winner.
causes: Not knowing what to do
Wanting an easy point without working
fixes: Play it only from inside the court, when you could hit a winner, to add a third option for the opponent.
outcome_effects: Loses the surprise and tactical value of the shot

good_form: Move your feet with intensity to get up to the short ball quickly.
Take the drop shot on the rise, as early as you can.
Moving forward makes the opponent back up, which sets up the drop shot.
Getting up close means the ball travels less distance and hangs in the air a shorter time.
Taking the ball on the rise lets you do very little with the racket: a small bunt with a slightly open face.
Racket face at contact is only about 10 degrees open, not wide open, and that gives enough backspin.
Make a slight grip change and feel the ball like a dropper.
Use a very short, simple swing.
Hitting the drop shot crosscourt against the opponent's body weight can force an error even if the depth is not great.
After hitting it, either stay back at three-quarter court between service line and baseline, or follow it in to the net if you took it early enough.
Shade toward the side you hit the drop shot to, since the crosscourt reply is the most common.
If they go slow down your line, you have time to lob or pass crosscourt; if they go short crosscourt, step up.
When coming in, stay balanced, cover the side you hit to, and be ready to pick off a volley on a diagonal.

faults.name: Drop shot from the baseline with no forward momentum
faults.looks_like: Getting a short ball but hitting the drop shot from back on the baseline without moving forward into it.
faults.why_it_matters: It is a harder shot to hit, and the opponent isn't backing up, so they are in a better position to run up to it.
causes: Not moving the feet quickly up to the short ball
fixes: Move forward with intensity to the ball and hit from about three-quarter court.
Take the ball on the rise.
outcome_effects: Opponent reaches the drop shot easily.
The ball must travel farther and hangs in the air longer, so the shot is less effective.

faults.name: Big hacking swing to create spin
faults.looks_like: Taking big hacks at the ball and trying to generate spin with the racket.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the shot harder; taking the ball early lets you do far less with the racket.
causes: No forward momentum
Taking the ball late instead of on the rise
fixes: Take the ball on the rise and bunt it with a slightly open face.
Use a short, simple swing.

faults.name: Racket face too wide open
faults.looks_like: Opening the racket face very wide at contact, thinking it has to be wide open.
faults.why_it_matters: Only a slight opening, about 10 degrees, is needed to give enough spin.
causes: Belief that the face must be wide open
fixes: Keep the face only about 10 degrees open at contact.

faults.name: Staying on the baseline after the drop shot
faults.looks_like: Hitting the drop shot and then remaining back on the baseline.
faults.why_it_matters: You are vulnerable to being drop-shotted back.
causes: Not planning what to do after the drop shot
fixes: Position at three-quarter court, shaded toward the crosscourt angle.
Or follow the shot into the net if you hit it early enough.
outcome_effects: Opponent can drop shot you right back.

faults.name: Waiting on the ball and hitting it as it drops
faults.looks_like: Letting the ball come down before hitting the drop shot, rather than moving up and taking it early (as with Begu's example where the ball was still dropping).
faults.why_it_matters: Taking it late gives the opponent time to reach the ball.
causes: Not moving up enough or early enough to the ball
fixes: Move up a little more and take the ball earlier, on the rise.
outcome_effects: The opponent gets to the drop shot.

faults.name: Too central positioning after the drop shot
faults.looks_like: Standing too close to the middle after the drop shot rather than shaded toward the side hit and the crosscourt angle.
faults.why_it_matters: The crosscourt reply is the common one, so you need to cover the angle and the line.
fixes: Shade a little further toward the side you hit to, and a bit closer to the net.
Cover the line and be ready to pick off the crosscourt reply on a diagonal.

good_form: Use a continental (hammer) grip, which lets you get under the ball.
Put a little backspin on the ball so the second bounce lands close to the first.
Come from behind and under the ball, hitting it from up to down.
Keep the swing short and soft, with no big swing, because the drop shot is a slow, short ball.
Hit it when you are stepping into the court in an offensive position, off an easy, short, soft or slightly high ball.
Prepare as if for an attacking shot, using your forehand or backhand grip, so your opponent steps back.
Wait as long as possible to change grip, which hides the shot.
Decide the direction before you hit. Go to one side and never down the middle, since the opponent has farther to run.
Aim between the net and the service line, roughly the middle of that zone, and not as short as possible.
Keep the ball low, with only enough height to clear the net.
A good drop shot has its second bounce inside the service line. The doubles alley is fine.
Step forward into the ball as you hit, ideally with the right leg on a forehand. This helps clear the net and gives momentum.
Follow the ball forward to the net as you would after an approach shot, and cover the court with diagonal movement.
Do not overuse it, and choose the right moment.

faults.name: Aiming too short
faults.looks_like: Trying to make the drop shot land as close to the net as possible, which sends the ball high into the air.
faults.why_it_matters: A high ball gives the opponent time to run to it and hit it after the bounce, and it leaves little margin for error.
causes: Trying to hit the drop shot as short as possible
fixes: Aim deeper, in the middle between the net and the service line.
Hit it from up to down so the ball travels low.
Use targets in the middle of that zone, and don't aim too fine.
outcome_effects: The ball floats high and the opponent has time to reach it.
The ball goes into the net.
Wind can catch the ball.
Aiming too fine can make the ball go out.

faults.name: Dropping the ball into the net by not stepping in
faults.looks_like: Hitting while staying still, so the ball is too soft and doesn't clear the net.
faults.why_it_matters: Missing in the net turns a point you were about to win into a point lost.
causes: Not stepping into the ball
Not enough power or momentum from the legs and body
fixes: Take a small step into the ball as you hit.
Step in, stop, change grip, then hit while stepping through.
outcome_effects: The ball goes too soft and into the net, giving away the point.

faults.name: Giving away the shot early
faults.looks_like: Running in with an open racket face and an early grip change.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent can tell a drop shot is coming.
causes: Changing grip too early
Preparing with an open racket face
fixes: Prepare with your normal forehand or backhand grip as if attacking.
Change grip at the last moment.
outcome_effects: The opponent expects the drop shot and is ready for it.

faults.name: Not following the drop shot to the net
faults.looks_like: Staying back after hitting, or not stepping through with the leg, so you push off late.
faults.why_it_matters: If the opponent reaches the ball, they get the offensive position at the net while you are stuck on the baseline.
causes: Treating the drop shot as a winner
Not stepping through with the leg as you hit
fixes: Step through with the leg so the momentum carries you forward.
Follow the ball and cover the court with diagonal movement.
Treat it as an approach shot.
outcome_effects: You react late.
The opponent gets the whole court to hit into, or can drop shot you back.

faults.name: Hitting it at the wrong moment
faults.looks_like: Playing a drop shot while moving backward, in defense, against a strong ball, or just out of tiredness or confusion.
faults.why_it_matters: It is not effective outside an offensive position.
causes: Throwing it in when tired or unsure what to do
Hitting it from a defensive position
fixes: Hit it when stepping into the court from an offensive, 'green' position.
Hold the rally longer if you are tired.
outcome_effects: The shot is less effective.

faults.name: Overusing the drop shot
faults.looks_like: Hitting too many drop shots.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent starts to read it, and it becomes the opposite of effective.
causes: Using it without picking the right moment
fixes: Use it only at the right moment and don't overdo it.
outcome_effects: The opponent anticipates the shot.

faults.name: Hitting down the middle
faults.looks_like: Placing the drop shot centrally.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent has less distance to run.
fixes: Pick a side before hitting.
outcome_effects: The opponent reaches the ball easily.

faults.name: Coming over the ball
faults.looks_like: Hitting over the ball and putting topspin on it.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball spins forward after the bounce toward the opponent coming in.
fixes: Use the continental grip and come under the ball for backspin.
outcome_effects: The ball kicks forward after bouncing, so the second bounce lands farther away.

good_form: Hit the drop shot when you are on attack, such as after a big serve or when the opponent is pushed back or on the run and has hit short, not when you are defending.
Hit from inside the baseline so the ball travels a shorter distance and the target is closer.
Use a Continental (chopper) grip to get underspin and control: base of the index knuckle and heel pad on bevel two.
Swing is like a slice but gentler: catch the bottom side of the ball rather than hitting through it, with the bottom edge of the racket going through contact.
Path is like a letter J: down, forward, then slightly up under the ball, still accelerating to create backspin without adding pace.
Keep soft hands, with a relaxed wrist and fingers, and the strings opening up towards the sky as if catching the ball on the strings.
Do not start the swing too early or fast; come up to the ball gently and stay close to it.
Aim for the ball's peak to be on your side of the net, and aim higher if you want more backspin.
The ideal result is a ball that bounces at least twice inside the service box, or stays in the box.
Disguise it: prepare as for a normal drive and change to Continental at the last second.
On a two-handed backhand, take the top hand off at the last moment because the bottom hand is already Continental.
On the forehand, change the grip with the fingers behind you late; a semi-Western player can twist just one bevel (like Alcaraz), and a Western player can rotate anticlockwise.
With a compact swing the free hand can help change grip; with a big backswing the change must happen late with the fingers.
Contact around chest or shoulder height so the ball needs less lift.
Move to the ball and get close so you can extend through it and feel it.

faults.name: Hitting drop shot while defending
faults.looks_like: Playing a drop shot when the opponent is attacking and you are on the defensive.
faults.why_it_matters: A good drop shot needs you to be attacking; in defense a neutralizing slice is the better choice.
causes: Choosing the wrong ball for the shot
fixes: Use the drop shot when you are set up to attack, the opponent is back on their heels, or after a big serve or big shot.

faults.name: Hitting through the ball like a slice
faults.looks_like: A long, linear swing showing lots of string to the ball, extending through contact.
faults.why_it_matters: A drop shot is a touch shot for finesse, not power.
causes: Swinging as in a normal slice, trying to add power and carry
fixes: Catch the underside of the ball gently with the bottom of the racket.
Use a J-shaped path, going down, forward and slightly up.
Keep soft hands and strings open to the sky.
outcome_effects: Ball carries too far and does not drop short
Opponent can reach it

faults.name: Gripping too tight
faults.looks_like: Rigid hand, tight grip on the racket, tense wrist and fingers.
faults.why_it_matters: Soft hands give the looseness at contact needed for touch.
fixes: Relax the wrist and fingers and hold the racket loosely.

faults.name: Changing grip too early
faults.looks_like: Switching to the chopper grip early, or waiting and running up to the ball with the racket already set for the drop shot.
faults.why_it_matters: The opponent senses something is off and anticipates the drop shot.
causes: Big swing or backswing making the change hard to do late
Not waiting until the last second to change
fixes: Prepare as for a normal drive and change at the last second.
Use the fingers to roll the grip behind you.
Use a compact swing so the free hand can help.
outcome_effects: Opponent anticipates and reaches the drop shot

faults.name: Hitting from too low
faults.looks_like: Making contact well below chest or shoulder height.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes good execution harder and gives the opponent more time.
fixes: Make contact around chest or shoulder height.
outcome_effects: Ball has to lift up first
Opponent gets more time

faults.name: Waiting for the ball or reaching
faults.looks_like: Standing still and letting the ball come, or reaching for it far out in front.
faults.why_it_matters: It gives the opponent time to recover, and the ball is hard to feel and control when too far in front.
causes: Not moving to the ball
fixes: Go to the ball, get close, and extend through it.
outcome_effects: More likely to miss
Opponent has time to recover

faults.name: Ball peak on opponent's side
faults.looks_like: The flight of the ball peaks after the net, on the opponent's side of the court.
faults.why_it_matters: It gives the opponent too much time to chase the ball down.
fixes: Make the peak of the ball flight on your side of the court; aim higher with more backspin.
outcome_effects: Opponent runs it down and catches it

good_form: Use the same setup and takeaway for the backhand drop shot as for the backhand slice, so the drop shot is disguised.
Take the racket back to about shoulder height on both shots.
The racket face comes in square, or close to square, on both shots.
The difference comes only at the very end: knife the ball deep for the slice, or fan the racket open with a lighter grip for the drop shot.
Hit deep, skidding backhand slices early in the match and rally to keep the opponent back near the baseline, which sets up the drop shot.
Generally don't open a match with drop shots.
Practice keeping the backswing position identical for both shots.

faults.name: Different setup telegraphs the drop shot
faults.looks_like: The backswing or takeaway for the drop shot looks different from the backhand slice, so the opponent can read it.
faults.why_it_matters: A perceptive opponent sees the setup and knows what is coming, so the drop shot loses its disguise and effectiveness.
causes: Backswing position for the drop shot does not match the slice backswing
Using the drop shot too early or without first showing deep slices
fixes: Make the backswing positions identical for both shots
Hit several deep backhand slices first so the opponent expects the same ball
Practice the same takeaway at shoulder height with a square racket face
outcome_effects: Opponent reads the shot and gets to it instead of letting it bounce twice

good_form: Think of the drop shot in aggressive terms, not as a bailout when you get a high ball.
Run around the ball and hold the disguise, making it look like your normal shot until the last second.
Change to a closer-to-weak Continental grip, similar to a forehand volley grip, as you come around the ball.
Think about curling the ball by getting to the inside of it.
Feel the racket outside your body to the side, coming across the ball and underneath it.
It is a feel-based shot.
It works best when the opponent is about 10 feet back or is a pusher.

faults.name: Treating the drop shot as a bailout
faults.looks_like: Taking a high ball and just dropping it or slicing it, without setting it up on purpose.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker wants the shot played in aggressive terms, and he says this mindset is the opposite of his approach.
causes: Seeing the drop shot only as a bailout for a high ball
fixes: Think of the drop shot aggressively and set it up deliberately.
Run around the ball and hold the disguise.

faults.name: Keeping the same grip through the shot
faults.looks_like: Running around the ball with the usual forehand grip, so the shot felt unnatural and came out badly.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker has the player change grip so the shot works. The first attempts looked bad.
causes: Not changing the grip as the player comes around the ball
fixes: Hold the disguise, then change to a weak Continental grip, like a forehand volley grip, as you come around the ball.
outcome_effects: The first attempt looked bad and unnatural.
